title: CertPool has no upper bound on pool size
description:
CertPool (pkix-path-builder/src/lib.rs) accepts an unbounded number of certificates via add() and FromIterator/Extend. The DFS path builder operates on this pool with a node-visit budget (DEFAULT_DFS_BUDGET = 10,000) that bounds CPU, but the memory consumed by the pool itself has no cap. An adversarial input (e.g., a CMS SignedData.certificates bag containing millions of valid Certificate values) can force unbounded heap allocation before the path builder ever runs.

What goes wrong (availability): Memory exhaustion / OOM before the DFS budget check is reached. The budget guards CPU time, not memory.

Locations:
- /home/mark/PROJECT/PKIX/pkix-path-builder/src/lib.rs lines 90-131 (CertPool::add, FromIterator, Extend)
- /home/mark/PROJECT/PKIX/pkix-chain/src/lib.rs line 603 (supplied_chain.iter().cloned().collect() into CertPool in build_with_aia)

Suggested fix: Add an optional max_certs field to PathBuilderConfig (default: something generous like 1000). CertPool::add / Extend / FromIterator could enforce a cap, or the builder functions could check pool.len() against config before proceeding. This is defense-in-depth -- callers controlling their own inputs are unaffected, but callers processing untrusted CMS bags get a bound.

Note: the DFS budget already mitigates the CPU side of adversarial pools. This finding is specifically about the memory side.
notes:
Analysis 2026-11-25: real but overstated and caller-owned. Dropped P1 -> P3 rather than closed; there is a constructive additive-API option below.

The decisive point is that CertPool does not amplify. It is literally `certs: Vec<Certificate>` and add() is a push (pkix-path-builder/src/lib.rs:86-100). No index, no derived structure. Memory is LINEAR in what the caller inserts.

That dismantles the stated attack. In the beads scenario -- a CMS SignedData.certificates bag with millions of entries -- the allocation happens when the CALLER parses that bag into Certificate values, because each one must already exist to be passed to add(). The OOM occurs in the DER parser, before CertPool is reached. A cap here would not prevent it; it would only reject certificates already materialised in memory, after the cost was paid.

The comparison the bead draws with DEFAULT_DFS_BUDGET actually argues against it. That budget exists because the DFS search is EXPONENTIAL in pool size -- genuine amplification, so a bound buys a lot. Pool storage is 1:1, so a bound buys only a different error message for an allocation the caller already made.

A cap would also have to be arbitrary and large. The crate feeds a 20,000-certificate pool in its own test (review_duplicate_decoys_are_deduplicated builds one from repeat_n(decoy, 20_000) and requires it to work), so any library-chosen limit must sit above that -- at which point it is not protecting against the millions-of-certs case any better than the host memory limit does.

Constructive option, if this is wanted: make the bound opt-in rather than imposed. A try_add returning an error, or a capacity-limited constructor, is additive and non-breaking, and lets a caller who is feeding untrusted CMS bags state their own limit while leaving callers with large legitimate pools alone. That is an API-design decision for you rather than something to pick unilaterally -- which is the same reason cr8.9/cr8.10 are parked.

Related: the AIA reassembly path, where certificates DO arrive from the network rather than from the caller, is separately bounded -- max_total_fetches (8) x max_certs_per_response (16) = 128 retained, plus URI and pool dedup. See PKIX-rm8.43, closed.
